items.title: Complex lattice and quotient torus
items.statement: A full complex lattice is Λ=Zω₁+Zω₂ with ω₁,ω₂ real-linearly independent; choose an oriented basis with Im(ω₂/ω₁)>0. The complex torus T_Λ is the quotient C/Λ with quotient topology and additive classes [z]. A different oriented basis of the same lattice differs by SL₂(Z).

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.strategy: Real-linear independence makes the generator map R²→C invertible, hence Λ is discrete and a closed fundamental parallelogram covers the quotient. Compare integer change-of-basis matrices: invertibility over Z gives determinant ±1, and positivity of the complex orientation selects +1. The next item constructs the quotient charts.

items.title: The quotient C/Λ is a compact Riemann surface
items.statement: Translation by Λ yields compatible complex charts on C/Λ, independent of representatives and oriented basis; the quotient is Hausdorff, second countable and compact, and C→C/Λ is a holomorphic covering map.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Choose ε below one third of the shortest nonzero lattice-vector length; translates of ε-discs are disjoint, giving evenly covered quotient discs and chart changes z↦z+λ. Distinct orbits have positive separation from the discrete lattice, so disjoint quotient neighbourhoods prove Hausdorffness. Images of rational-centred rational-radius discs form a countable base because the orbit map is open. A closed basis parallelogram maps onto the quotient, proving compactness. Any two quotient points are joined by the image of their lifts’ straight segment, so the torus is path connected and hence connected. Only finite and explicitly indexed choices are used.

items.title: Weierstrass ℘ function
items.statement: For a full lattice Λ define ℘_Λ(z)=z⁻²+Σ_{ω∈Λ\{0}}((z−ω)⁻²−ω⁻²), where the sum is the absolutely convergent finite-subset sum on compact sets off Λ. The term z⁻² fixes the principal part and the subtractions fix zero constant term at 0.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.strategy: For |ω|>2 sup_K|z| expand the summand as 2zω⁻³+O_K(|ω|⁻⁴). Annular lattice point counts O(R²) make Σ|ω|⁻³ finite, so the series is independent of enumeration; the following theorem proves the full normal-convergence and ellipticity claim.

items.title: Elliptic function for a lattice
items.statement: A Λ-elliptic function is a meromorphic f on C with f(z+λ)=f(z) for every λ∈Λ, with equality as sphere-valued maps at poles. Equivalently it is a meromorphic function on T_Λ via the quotient charts.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.strategy: The quotient covering charts make a periodic meromorphic function descend uniquely; changing a representative translates its germ, so the pole order and meromorphicity agree. Conversely pull back a torus-meromorphic function along the quotient map.

items.title: Weierstrass ζ and σ functions
items.statement: For Λ define ζ_Λ(z)=z⁻¹+Σ_{ω≠0}((z−ω)⁻¹+ω⁻¹+zω⁻²) and σ_Λ(z)=z∏_{ω≠0}(1−z/ω)exp(z/ω+z²/(2ω²)). For a primitive period ω let η_ω=2ζ_Λ(ω/2); the quasi-period claims ζ(z+ω)=ζ(z)+η_ω and σ(z+ω)=−exp(η_ω(z+ω/2))σ(z) are proved in the subsequent theorem.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.strategy: The summands and E₂-product factors have O_K(|ω|⁻³) tails, using the lattice count from the ℘ definition. Thus both are normally convergent off their prescribed zeros/poles. Primitive means part of an integer lattice basis; the constants are basis-specific but the functions depend only on Λ.

items.title: Normal convergence, parity and periodicity of ℘
items.statement: The ℘ series converges absolutely and normally off Λ, independently of enumeration. It is even and Λ-periodic, with one double pole of principal part (z−ω)⁻² at each lattice point and no other poles; ℘′(z)=−2Σ_{ω∈Λ}(z−ω)⁻³ is odd and elliptic.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Bound each paired or unpaired tail on a compact K by C_K|ω|⁻³ and count O(R²) points in a radius-R lattice disc; the dyadic sum is geometric. Local uniform convergence permits derivative summation. The derivative series is absolutely convergent and reindexes under each lattice translation. Hence ℘(z+ω_j)−℘(z) is constant; evenness from ω↦−ω makes it zero at z=−ω_j/2. Translate the expansion at 0 to each lattice point; its constant term vanishes by the subtractions.

items.title: Divisor and residue laws for elliptic functions
items.statement: For a nonconstant Λ-elliptic f and any translated fundamental parallelogram whose boundary avoids its zeros and poles, the numbers of zeros and poles in its interior agree with multiplicity and the sum of residues of f there is zero. Both totals and the residue sum are independent of the translated boundary; in particular an elliptic function with no poles is constant and a nonconstant one has at least two poles counted with multiplicity.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: The torus has finite zero and pole sets by isolation and compactness; choose a generic translated boundary missing them. Integrate f′/f and f round it. Opposite edge integrals cancel by periodicity, while the planar argument and residue principles give zero-minus-pole count and residue sum. Any two such parallelograms represent every torus point once, so totals are translate-independent. A pole-free f is bounded on one closed parallelogram and globally by periodicity, hence constant; a single simple pole would have nonzero residue, contradicting the residue sum.

items.title: Convergence, zeros and quasi-periods of ζ and σ
items.statement: The ζ series is meromorphic, odd, with simple lattice poles of residue 1, and ζ′=−℘. The σ product is entire, odd, has exactly simple lattice zeros, σ′/σ=ζ and σ′(0)=1. For an oriented basis (ω₁,ω₂), η_j=2ζ(ω_j/2) satisfies ζ(z+ω_j)=ζ(z)+η_j and σ(z+ω_j)=−e^{η_j(z+ω_j/2)}σ(z), and η₁ω₂−η₂ω₁=2πi.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Use O_K(|ω|⁻³) tails to pass derivatives through both the series and E₂ product. Factor each zero through one factor and a nonzero normal tail; pairing ±ω gives oddness. Termwise differentiation proves ζ′=−℘ and logarithmic differentiation proves σ′/σ=ζ. Periodicity of ℘ makes ζ(z+ω_j)−ζ(z) constant, and oddness at −ω_j/2 gives 2ζ(ω_j/2). Integrate the logarithmic derivative of σ(z+ω_j)/σ(z) and use σ odd at −ω_j/2 to fix the factor −1. A translated boundary-free parallelogram contains one ζ pole; the contour residue formula and opposite-edge differences give the stated Legendre relation. All constants match the full-period rather than half-period convention.

items.title: Weierstrass cubic differential equation
items.statement: For G₄(Λ)=Σ_{ω≠0}ω⁻⁴ and G₆(Λ)=Σ_{ω≠0}ω⁻⁶, put g₂=60G₄ and g₃=140G₆. These sums converge absolutely and (℘′)²=4℘³−g₂℘−g₃ as elliptic meromorphic functions.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Expand ℘ at 0 by termwise geometric series: ℘=z⁻²+3G₄z²+5G₆z⁴+O(z⁶), ℘′=−2z⁻³+6G₄z+20G₆z³+O(z⁵). The displayed difference has no principal part and zero constant term. It is elliptic and has no possible poles away from Λ, so the pole-free consequence of the divisor law makes it constant, and its limit at 0 makes it zero.

items.title: Degree two of ℘ and its four branch points
items.statement: The meromorphic map ℘:T_Λ→Ĉ has degree two, and ℘(z)=℘(w) exactly when w≡z or −z mod Λ. Its branch points are 0 and the three distinct nonzero classes ω₁/2, ω₂/2, (ω₁+ω₂)/2; ℘′ has exactly one simple zero at each nonzero half-period and no others modulo Λ.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: The single double pole gives weighted fibre count two over ∞; compactness makes ℘ proper, so the published degree theorem gives degree two everywhere. Evenness supplies the pair z,−z; if distinct they exhaust the fibre. At each nonzero 2-torsion point, oddness and periodicity force ℘′=0. Its unique triple pole at 0 makes the zero count three by the divisor law, so those three zeros are all simple. The local order of ℘−℘(h) is two at each h, giving the branch points; at 0 the sphere coordinate 1/℘ is z²+O(z⁶).

items.title: Addition formula for ℘
items.statement: Meromorphically in (z,w), ℘(z+w)=−℘(z)−℘(w)+¼((℘′(z)−℘′(w))/(℘(z)−℘(w)))² wherever the displayed quotient is initially defined; all apparent exceptional cases are interpreted by meromorphic continuation.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: First fix generic w with 2w∉Λ and ℘′(w)≠0. As a function of z the right side is elliptic. The degree-two fibre lemma shows denominator zeros occur only at z=±w; at z=w numerator also vanishes and the singularity is removable, while at z=−w Laurent expansion gives exactly the double principal part of ℘(z+w). At z=0 the z⁻² terms cancel and the finite limit equals ℘(w), fixing the remaining constant. Thus the two elliptic functions agree. The identity theorem in w extends through half-period and coincident-denominator cases, as an equality of meromorphic functions, without asserting a finite value at actual poles.

items.title: The field of elliptic functions is C(℘,℘′)
items.statement: Every Λ-elliptic meromorphic function is a rational expression in ℘_Λ and ℘′_Λ. More precisely K(T_Λ)=C(℘,℘′), with the cubic relation (℘′)²=4℘³−g₂℘−g₃.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Split f into even and odd parts. An even elliptic function is constant on the degree-two fibres of ℘, so it descends meromorphically through local power-map coordinates, including all four branch points, to a meromorphic sphere function; the published sphere theorem makes that rational in ℘. For the odd part, f_odd/℘′ is even; at a half-period both are odd in a centred local coordinate, so the quotient remains meromorphic. Thus f=R(℘)+℘′S(℘). The differential equation supplies the claimed algebraic relation; no Riemann–Roch or group law is imported.

items.title: Nonvanishing of the lattice discriminant
items.statement: For a full lattice Λ, Δ(Λ)=g₂(Λ)³−27g₃(Λ)² is nonzero. The polynomial 4x³−g₂x−g₃ has three distinct roots e_j=℘(h_j) at the three nonzero half-periods h_j, so the projective cubic Y²Z=4X³−g₂XZ²−g₃Z³ is smooth, including at its unique point at infinity.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: At each nonzero half-period h_j the lemma makes ℘′ zero and ℘−e_j have a double zero, exhausting its degree-two fibre. Hence distinct h_j have distinct e_j. Substituting ℘′(h_j)=0 into the differential equation gives three distinct roots of the cubic; its algebraic discriminant is g₂³−27g₃² up to a nonzero scalar, so Δ≠0. An affine singular point would require y=0 and a repeated root of the cubic, impossible. At Z=0 the cubic forces X=0, giving only O=[0:1:0]. In chart Y=1 with u=X/Y and v=Z/Y, the equation is v−4u³+g₂uv²+g₃v³=0 and its v-derivative at (0,0) is 1; the holomorphic implicit-function theorem supplies a smooth local chart there. This proves smoothness before any use of the cubic isomorphism.

items.title: Uniformization of the nonsingular Weierstrass cubic
items.statement: The map [z]↦[℘(z):℘′(z):1] for z∉Λ extends at [0] to [0:1:0] and gives a biholomorphism T_Λ≅{[X:Y:Z]∈CP²:Y²Z=4X³−g₂XZ²−g₃Z³}. The cubic is smooth, including at its unique point at infinity.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: The differential equation puts the affine image on the cubic. Δ≠0 rules out affine singularities. At Z=0 the equation forces X=0, giving O=[0:1:0]; in chart Y=1 set u=X/Y,v=Z/Y, obtaining v=4u³−g₂uv²−g₃v³ with ∂/∂v=1 at O. Thus u is a holomorphic coordinate there. Near z=0, u=℘/℘′=−z/2+O(z⁵) and v=1/℘′=−z³/2+O(z⁷), so the map extends and has nonzero local derivative. The map is injective: degree two and evenness give the only potential collision z and −z; ℘′ has opposite signs and vanishes only where those are already the same torus point. For each finite cubic point (x,y), the proper degree-two ℘ map is onto Ĉ, so choose z with ℘(z)=x; the differential equation gives ℘′(z)=±y, and replacing z by −z picks the desired sign when y≠0. When y=0, x is one of the three distinct half-period values and its unique preimage has ℘′=0. The sole infinity point is the image of 0. Thus the map is surjective without assuming connectedness of the algebraic curve. The torus is connected by the quotient theorem, so its continuous surjective image, the smooth cubic, is connected. It is therefore a bijective holomorphic map between Riemann surfaces; the local normal form forces degree one at every point and hence a holomorphic inverse.

items.title: The chord-tangent group law and elliptic uniformization
items.statement: Let C_Λ be the smooth projective cubic Y²Z=4X³−g₂XZ²−g₃Z³, O=[0:1:0], and Φ([z])=[℘(z):℘′(z):1] with Φ(0)=O. Transport addition from T_Λ to C_Λ through Φ and call it ⊕. For every projective line L, if L·C_Λ=Q₁+Q₂+Q₃ is its intersection divisor, with tangent and other repeated intersections counted with multiplicity, then Q₁⊕Q₂⊕Q₃=O. Thus the transported operation is the chord-tangent law: for a secant or tangent whose third intersection is R, P⊕Q=−R; vertical lines give P,−P,O (with multiplicity two at a half-period point), and the line at infinity cuts out 3O. In particular Φ([z]+[w])=Φ([z])⊕Φ([w]), so Φ is a group isomorphism.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, p. 47, Proposition 3.12 continuation
C. T. McMullen, Advanced Complex Analysis, Math 213a notes (2010), Ch. 5, Theorem 5.16 and Corollaries 5.17–5.20, printed pp. 89–90
C. T. McMullen, Advanced Complex Analysis, Math 213a notes (2 Dec 2025), Ch. 5 §5.2, Theorem 5.16 and Corollaries 5.17–5.20, pp. 148–150

items.proof_strategy: First define ⊕ by transporting the already-defined additive law of T_Λ through the biholomorphism Φ; this supplies associativity and the identity without assuming any cubic group law. For generic z,w with finite distinct nonvertical images, put x=℘(z), y=℘′(z), u=℘(w), v=℘′(w), m=(v−y)/(u−x), and t=℘(z+w). The ℘ addition identity gives t=m²/4−x−u, which is the third x-coordinate by Vieta after intersecting Y=mX+b with the cubic. Differentiate the addition identity in z. The cubic equation gives ℘″(z)=6x²−g₂/2, while v²−y²=(u−x)(4(u²+ux+x²)−g₂). Since v−y=m(u−x), this gives m²(u−x)+2my=4(u²+ux+x²)−g₂. Together with ℘″(z)=6x²−g₂/2 and t=m²/4−x−u, this rearranges to my−℘″(z)=2(u−x)(x−t), hence m_z=2(x−t). Hence ℘′(z+w)=m(x−t)−y, so the third line point has y-coordinate y+m(t−x)=−℘′(z+w), namely R=Φ(−z−w). Evenness of ℘ and oddness of ℘′ give the cubic reflection −Φ(s)=Φ(−s), so −R=Φ(z+w)=Φ(z)⊕Φ(w). Thus a generic line divisor P+Q+R has transported sum O and its secant operation agrees with ⊕; this proves agreement directly from the analytic identity, without presupposing a cubic group law. Letting w tend to z makes the secant tend to the tangent at P=Φ(z); the two coalescing intersections count as 2P and the residual point is Φ(−2z), so 2P+Φ(−2z) has transported sum O. If Φ(−2z)=P, equivalently 3[z]=0, the tangent has triple intersection 3P. At a half-period the tangent is vertical and is included below. A vertical line x=c cuts P,−P,O, with O simple (in the infinity chart its equation is u=cv and u=−z/2+O(z⁵)); when P=−P at a half-period, the finite intersection is 2P. Finally the line at infinity cuts out 3O: in the existing infinity chart u=X/Y is a local coordinate, and v=Z/Y=−z³/2+O(z⁷) has order three, so the full line-divisor sum is O. Every projective line is nonvertical affine, vertical, or the line at infinity; the secant, tangent, and these exceptional cases establish the stated sum for every intersection divisor with multiplicity. Since ⊕ was transported, associativity follows from T_Λ after this agreement is proved, and Φ is a group isomorphism.

title: Elliptic Functions and Complex Tori: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Oriented bases and SL₂(Z)
items.statement: For Λ=Z+iZ the bases (1,i) and (1+i,i) have the same positive complex orientation and differ by a determinant-one integer matrix, while (i,1) reverses orientation. All yield the same quotient torus.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Write each new basis in the old one, calculate determinants 1 and −1, and check Im(ω₂/ω₁)>0 for the first two. The quotient set, covering charts and group law depend on Λ itself, not the chosen basis.

items.title: Moving the boundary of a fundamental parallelogram
items.statement: For ℘ on Λ=Z+iZ the parallelogram based at a=(1+i)/4 has no pole on its boundary, whereas the unshifted one has a pole at its vertices; for any nonzero elliptic f a generic translate avoids its finite torus divisor.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: The four edges of a+[0,1]+i[0,1] have a real or imaginary coordinate equal to 1/4 or 5/4, hence contain no integer lattice point. For arbitrary f the finitely many divisor classes forbid only finitely many translated edge arcs in a small open disc of possible basepoints; choose a point off those arcs and apply the divisor law.

items.title: Square and hexagonal lattice invariants
items.statement: For Λ_sq=Z+iZ, g₃(Λ_sq)=0 and g₂(Λ_sq)≠0. For Λ_hex=Z+Zρ with ρ=e^{2πi/3}, g₂(Λ_hex)=0 and g₃(Λ_hex)≠0; in both cases Δ≠0.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Absolute convergence permits reindexing Eisenstein sums. iΛ_sq=Λ_sq gives g₃=i⁻⁶g₃=−g₃, hence zero. ρΛ_hex=Λ_hex gives g₂=ρ⁻⁴g₂=ρ²g₂, hence zero. Nonvanishing of Δ forces the other invariant to be nonzero. No numerical evaluation of either sum is claimed.

items.title: Half-period values of the square lattice
items.statement: On Λ=Z+iZ, h=(1+i)/2 has ℘(h)=0; the other two nonzero half-period values are the distinct roots ±√g₂/2 of 4x³−g₂x. The four branch values of ℘ are 0, ±√g₂/2 and ∞.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: The scaling identity from the defining series gives ℘(iz)=−℘(z) on the square lattice. Since ih≡h mod Λ, ℘(h)=0. The cubic with g₃=0 has the displayed remaining roots; the nonzero discriminant makes them distinct. The degree-two lemma identifies exactly these finite branch values plus ∞.

items.title: Addition and duplication for ℘
items.statement: For generic z, ℘(2z)=−2℘(z)+¼(℘″(z)/℘′(z))²; equivalently ℘″=6℘²−g₂/2 makes it a rational expression in ℘ and ℘′. Both identities extend meromorphically through their apparent exceptional points.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: Take w→z in the addition formula where ℘′(z)≠0 and apply the derivative quotient limit. Differentiate the cubic identity; divide by 2℘′ on its nonzero locus to get ℘″=6℘²−g₂/2. Meromorphic identity then extends both formulas across zeros of ℘′ without assigning a finite value to genuine poles.

items.title: A simple zero of σ on the square lattice
items.statement: For Λ=Z+iZ, σ_Λ(0)=σ_Λ(1)=0, σ′_Λ(0)=1 and σ′_Λ(1)=−exp(η₁/2)≠0 where η₁=2ζ_Λ(1/2); these zeros are simple, while ζ has residue 1 at both points.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: The product gives σ(z)=z(1+O(z³)) near 0. Differentiate σ(z+1)=−e^{η₁(z+1/2)}σ(z) at z=0 to obtain the derivative at 1. The zeta quasi-period and its pole at 0 give residue 1 at 1. This concrete calculation displays the lattice-zero convention.

items.title: A singular cubic outside the lattice family
items.statement: The projective cubic Y²Z=4X³−3XZ²−Z³ has Δ=3³−27·1²=0 and an affine singular point (x,y)=(−1/2,0). It is a degeneration for orientation only and supplies no dependency for a lattice theorem.

references.title: J. S. Milne, Modular Functions and Modular Forms, Ch. 3, pp. 41–47
C. T. McMullen, Math 213a Advanced Complex Analysis, Ch. 5 §5.1, pp. 79–90
NIST DLMF §23.2, Definitions and Periodic Properties, equations 23.2.1–17

items.proof_strategy: In the affine chart factor 4x³−3x−1=(x−1)(2x+1)². At x=−1/2 and y=0, the defining polynomial and both partial derivatives vanish; Δ=0. The lattice theorem excludes these coefficients for any full Λ. This example is terminal and cannot be cited as a supplier.

items.title: Rectangular lattices, real mapping, and inverse elliptic integrals
items.statement: Let Λ=Zα+Zβ with α>0 real and β∈iR_{>0}, c₁=α/2, c₂=β/2, c₃=(α+β)/2, and e_j=℘(c_j), ordered e₂<e₃<e₁. Then ℘(z) is real exactly on the horizontal and vertical lines through Λ/2, and its restriction to a half-period rectangle maps conformally onto one half-plane. Every inverse branch satisfies dz/dζ=(4ζ³−g₂ζ−g₃)^(−1/2), giving α/2=∫_{e₁}^{∞}dx/√(4x³−g₂x−g₃)=∫_{e₂}^{e₃}dx/√(4x³−g₂x−g₃) and β/(2i)=∫_{−∞}^{e₂}dx/√(g₃+g₂x−4x³)=∫_{e₃}^{e₁}dx/√(g₃+g₂x−4x³), with positive real square roots. In the corresponding Jacobi example, for 0<k<1 put K(a)=∫₀¹ds/√((1−s²)(1−a²s²)), K=K(k), and K′=K(√(1−k²)); I_k(z)=∫₀ᶻdζ/√((1−ζ²)(1−k²ζ²)) maps the upper half-plane conformally to the rectangle with vertices −K,K,K+iK′,−K+iK′; its inverse sn extends by reflection to a doubly periodic meromorphic function with periods 4K and 2iK′.

references.title: C. T. McMullen, Advanced Complex Analysis, Math 213a notes (2 Dec 2025), Ch. 5 §5.3, Theorems 5.21–5.25, pp. 152–155
Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, Complex Analysis, Ch. 8 §4.5, pp. 245–247

items.proof_strategy: For rectangular Λ, conjugating the normally convergent defining series gives ℘(̅z)=overline{℘(z)}. If ℘(z) is real, then ℘(z)=℘(̅z), and the degree-two fibre lemma forces ̅z≡z or −z mod Λ; these are exactly the half-lattice horizontal and vertical lines. The branch points bound a rectangle S; ℘ has no critical point in its interior, its boundary maps to the extended real line, and the degree-two fibre criterion makes ℘|S injective, hence conformal onto a half-plane. For an inverse f, differentiate ℘(f(ζ))=ζ and use the cubic differential equation to obtain f′(ζ)=1/√(4ζ³−g₂ζ−g₃); integrate along the real boundary edges of S. The critical values are the ordered real roots e₂<e₃<e₁, and the two edge paths to the branch points give the displayed real period integrals; the alternate interval integrals agree by deforming the corresponding paths around the same two branch values. For the Jacobi integral choose the analytic square-root branch in the upper half-plane. Its derivative has no zero there; evaluating the boundary integrals on the four real intervals cut by −1/k,−1,1,1/k gives horizontal rectangle edges of length 2K and vertical edges of length K′. These are the side lengths before reflection; the successive reflections produce periods 4K and 2iK′. The argument principle shows that the map has degree one over the rectangle, hence is conformal. Its inverse is real on the straight edges after the appropriate affine normalization, so the holomorphic Schwarz reflection principle continues it across each edge; successive reflections give sn(z+2iK′)=sn(z) and sn(z+4K)=sn(z).

items.title: The rank-one cotangent and its conic
items.statement: Put P(z)=πcot(πz) and q=e^(2πiz). The exponential induces C/Z≅C*, and P(z)=πi(q+1)/(q−1) identifies C/Z biholomorphically with Ĉ minus {−iπ,iπ}. For finite values x=P(z), y=−P′(z), the identity −P′=P²+π² puts (x,y) on the affine conic y=x²+π². The map z↦[P(z):−P′(z):1] extends at the unique pole modulo Z to [0:1:0] on its projective closure YZ=X²+π²Z², and identifies C/Z with that conic minus the two points [−iπ:0:1] and [iπ:0:1]. The function P has exact period 1 and principal part 1/z at 0, making this the rank-one analogue of lattice uniformization.

references.title: C. T. McMullen, Advanced Complex Analysis, Math 213a notes (2 Dec 2025), Ch. 5 §5.4, Theorems 5.26–5.27, pp. 156–157

items.proof_strategy: The exponential q=e^(2πiz) has kernel Z and induces C/Z≅C*. The identity cot(πz)=i(q+1)/(q−1) identifies P with the Möbius map q↦πi(q+1)/(q−1), whose omitted values are ±iπ; q=1 maps to infinity. Differentiating the cotangent and using csc²=1+cot² gives −P′=P²+π². Near z=0, P=1/z+O(z) and −P′=1/z²+O(1), so [P:−P′:1] extends holomorphically to [0:1:0] on the projective conic YZ=X²+π²Z². The projective conic is parametrized by x: finite x determines the unique point y=x²+π², and x=∞ is [0:1:0]. Thus the Möbius bijection gives its image with the two points over x=±iπ removed. Since the Möbius transform is injective, P(z+T)=P(z) iff e^(2πiT)=1, so its full period group is Z. The published partial-fraction expansion supplies the principal part and symmetric integer-pole sum.

items.title: A canonical reduced basis for a complex lattice
items.statement: Every full complex lattice Λ admits an oriented basis (ω₁,ω₂) whose ratio τ=ω₂/ω₁ satisfies Imτ>0, −1/2<Reτ≤1/2, |τ|≥1, and Reτ≥0 when |τ|=1. This reduced ratio is uniquely determined by Λ. The oriented bases realizing it are two generically, four when τ=i (the square lattice), and six when τ=e^(iπ/3) (the hexagonal lattice).

references.title: L. V. Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 7 §2.3, Theorem 2, pp. 268–269

items.proof_strategy: Choose a shortest nonzero lattice vector ω₁; it is primitive and therefore extends to a basis. Choose the orientation and replace a complementary vector ω₂ by ω₂+nω₁ so that |Re(ω₂/ω₁)|≤1/2. The shortest-vector property gives |ω₂|≥|ω₁| and |ω₁±ω₂|≥|ω₁|, hence |τ|≥1 and the centered real-part bound. Boundary basis changes put τ into −1/2<Reτ≤1/2 and Reτ≥0 when |τ|=1. For uniqueness compare any two such ratios by τ′=(aτ+b)/(cτ+d), ad−bc=1; Imτ′=Imτ/|cτ+d|² and the defining inequalities leave only τ′=τ, with stabilizers at i and e^(πi/3) giving the square and hexagonal multiplicities. This is a canonical ratio, not a claim that the oriented basis itself is always unique.
